newsitem.title: USA: US Rep. Castle sees support for separate tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: US Rep. Castle sees support for separate tax cuts.

text.p: Support was growing among House Republicans for the strategy of considering tax cuts after balancing the budget, but the majority still preferred keeping the two together, Rep. Michael Castle said Wednesday.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, early last week angered members of his party by suggesting delaying consideration of tax cuts until after balancing the budget.
Gingrich spent the rest of the week trying to reassure those who took offense that he was talking only about a strategic maneuver and was firmly committed to cutting taxes.

Castle, a Delaware Republican, said about 70 Republicans supported separating tax cuts from balancing the budget. However, the majority of Republicans would still prefer to see tax cuts as part of a budget plan, Castle said.

"If you took it to a vote of the conference they would probably prefer still, even a majority, although not a big majority any more, would prefer to have tax cuts included," Castle said at a press conference.

He was one of 19 members of a House Republican coaltion, the Mainstream Conservative Alliance, who sent a letter to Gingrich and other leaders supporting separating consideration of budget balancing and tax reduction.
"We're in the rough range of 70...Republican members of Congress who have now signed one letter or another indicating that we should have separation," Castle said.
"All this suggests that there is a growing consensus that only if we concentrate on balancing the budget first can we achieve both goals of balancing the budget and providing tax cuts," he said.
Castle outlined his own budget plan, saying it was a compromise between President Clinton's budget proposal for fiscal 1998 and the Republican budget plan for fiscal 1997.
The plan would use spending cuts and no tax increases to balance the budget and then separately have tax cuts paid for mainly by the "fiscal dividend" from a budget deal, he said.
The fiscal dividend assumes that a balanced budget agreement would result in lower interest rates, higher economic growth, and lower costs for the federal government for interest payments on debt.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated a "fiscal dividend" of $77 billion over five years if a budget agreement was reached in time for 1998, Castle said.
Staff from the White House and congressional budget committees have been meeting this week in preparing groundwork for budget negotiations expected to start after Congress returns from Spring recess.
Castle said he expected the House budget committee plan would include both a balanced budget and tax cuts.
Rick May, chief of staff of the House Budget Committee, would not comment on the current staff budget discussions.
Asked if the committee was pursuing a specific tax cut goal, May said it was "too premature" to talk about specific numbers.
"We are still looking at options, we are still looking at various ideas and proposals and suggestions and we have not made any final decisions about anything," May said.
